text:
To: All Staff
From: Ingrid Solberg, Chief Executive
Subject: Proposed acquisition of Veldt Logistics

I am writing to inform you that the board has entered into exclusive talks to acquire Veldt Logistics, a transport specialist with operations in nine countries. No agreement has yet been signed, and the transaction remains [1] to regulatory approval, which we do not expect before the autumn.

[2] Until the position is clear, the two companies will continue to operate independently, and our own customers should notice no change in the service they receive. [3] the acquisition proceeds, we anticipate a period of integration lasting up to eighteen months, during which some roles may be reorganized. I recognize that uncertainty is unwelcome, and I undertake to [4] you promptly of every significant development.

questions.explanation: 'Remains subject to regulatory approval' is the fixed expression; 'subjected' and 'subjecting' need an object or 'to' after a different structure, and 'subjective' has an unrelated meaning.

choices: Staff are therefore asked to refrain from questioning the proposal within the company while negotiations are under way.
Staff are therefore asked to refrain from discussing the proposal outside the company while negotiations are under way.
Staff were therefore asked to discuss the proposal outside the company after negotiations had been concluded.
Customers are therefore asked to refrain from discussing the proposal outside the company while negotiations are under way.
questions.explanation: The next sentence begins 'Until the position is clear', continuing an instruction about the interim period; the first option asks for discretion during negotiations. The others discourage internal questions, use a past tense inconsistent with the announcement, or address customers instead of staff.
'In the event that the acquisition proceeds' introduces a possible future development; 'inasmuch as' would state it as an established fact, and 'notwithstanding that' and 'albeit' express concession.
'Apprise you of' means to inform you of; 'comprise', 'surprise' and 'enterprise' have different meanings and structures.

text:
Ageing Workforce Forces Manufacturers to Rethink Training

Across the engineering sector, firms are confronting a demographic problem that has been building for decades: nearly a third of skilled machinists are due to retire within ten years, and too few young people are entering the trade to replace them. Employers' associations have long urged schools to [1] vocational pathways, but progress has been slow.

[2] A growing number of companies are therefore taking matters into their own hands. Bradfield Precision, for instance, now runs a four-year apprenticeship that combines paid work on the shop floor with study at a local college. [3] the scheme is costly, its managing director argues that the expense is modest compared with the loss of expertise that retirements would entail. Critics counter that such programs benefit only large firms, [4] smaller workshops lack the resources to release staff for training.

questions.explanation: Associations urge schools to 'promote' (encourage) vocational pathways; 'provoke', 'prosecute' and 'prolong' do not take 'pathways' as a sensible object.

choices: Waiting for the education system to widen this gap is, in the view of many executives, no longer a realistic option.
Waiting for the education system to close this gap is, in the view of many executives, no longer a realistic option.
Waiting for retirements to close this gap was, in the view of many executives, not a realistic option.
Relying on the education system to close this gap is, in the view of many apprentices, still a realistic option.
questions.explanation: The next sentence says 'A growing number of companies are therefore taking matters into their own hands', so the preceding one must say that waiting for schools is not viable. The others reverse the logic, shift the subject to retirements or declare the school route realistic.
'Although the scheme is costly' concedes a drawback before the managing director's defense; 'because' would explain the cost wrongly, and 'unless' and 'whenever' do not fit.
'Whereas smaller workshops lack the resources' contrasts large firms with small ones; 'therefore', 'moreover' and 'hence' do not mark contrast.

text:
Dear Mr. Brandvold,

Further to our meeting on 14 May, I am writing to set out the terms on which Halvorsen & Dale would be willing to renew the lease of Unit 6, Harbour Point. The proposed term is five years from 1 September, with a rent review at the end of the third year. [1] The current rent of £86,000 per annum would remain unchanged for the first twenty-four months.

We would, however, wish to introduce a break clause exercisable by either party on six months' notice after the second anniversary. [2] such a clause would give both sides valuable flexibility, we appreciate that it may be unwelcome to a tenant who has invested heavily in the premises. We would therefore be [3] to discuss a modest contribution toward your fit-out costs, [4] you agree to a minimum term of three years.

Yours sincerely,
Helen Pryce
Property Manager

choices: This offer is made subject to contract and to the satisfactory completion of a survey of the building.
This offer is made subject to contract and to the satisfactory completion of a survey of the tenant.
This offer was made subject to contract and to the unsatisfactory completion of a survey of the building.
This request is made subject to inspection and to the satisfactory completion of a lease of the building.
questions.explanation: The following sentence ('The current rent ... would remain unchanged') continues the terms of the offer; the first option frames those terms as conditional. The others contain an illogical object ('survey of the tenant'), a contradictory tense and adjective, or confuse an offer with a request.

'While such a clause would give both sides valuable flexibility, we appreciate that ...' concedes a benefit before a drawback; 'because' and 'since' give reasons that do not make sense, and 'provided' needs 'that'.
'We would therefore be prepared to discuss' uses the adjective 'prepared' followed by 'to'; the other forms do not follow 'be'.
'Provided that you agree' sets the condition for the contribution; 'as though', 'even if' and 'in case' contradict or misrepresent the condition.

text:
SECURITY ADVISORY – IMMEDIATE ACTION REQUIRED

Our monitoring systems have detected a series of fraudulent e-mails purporting to come from the finance department and requesting urgent changes to supplier bank details. [1] Employees should therefore not act on any such request unless it has been [2] by telephone, using a number held on file rather than one supplied in the message.

[3], any employee who has already responded to a message of this kind must contact the security desk without delay, so that the transaction can be recalled where possible. The firm will [4] a mandatory briefing on fraud awareness on 9 June.

choices: Several of the messages have proved convincing enough to prompt a payment of £37,000 before the deception was discovered.
Most of the messages were intercepted by the mail filter before they could reach any employee mailbox at all.
The finance department has since replaced the telephone number held on file for each supplier in its records.
None of the messages has yet resulted in a payment, although their number has risen sharply in recent days.
questions.explanation: The next sentence says employees should 'therefore' not act on such requests, so the previous sentence must establish a real danger. Only the first does; the others say the messages were intercepted, change the contact details, or report that no payment has occurred.
A request is 'verified' by calling a known number; 'certified' implies an official document, 'justified' means given a reason, and 'rectified' means corrected.
The sentence adds a second instruction to the first; 'conversely' and 'nonetheless' mark contrast, and 'thereafter' marks a later time.
A firm can 'convene' a briefing (call it together); 'convey' needs a message as its object, 'converge' is intransitive, and 'convert' means change.

text:
To: Senior Managers
From: Philippa Greaves, Director of Human Resources
Subject: Revised relocation policy

The company's relocation policy has been revised in the light of last year's experience, when several transfers were delayed by disputes over costs. The new policy applies to all internal transfers requiring a move of more than eighty kilometers, [1] of grade.

[2] Employees will receive a lump sum covering removal and temporary accommodation, rather than reimbursement of individual receipts. [3] a transferred employee leaves the company within two years of the move, a proportion of the lump sum must be repaid. Managers are asked to [4] their teams about these terms before any transfer is discussed.

questions.explanation: 'Irrespective of their role' is the fixed expression meaning without regard to; 'notwithstanding', 'apart' and 'aside' are not followed by 'of' in this sense.

choices: The aim is to speed up the processing of receipts, which previously took several weeks to be approved by the company.
The aim is to remove the uncertainty that previously arose when employees and the company interpreted eligible expenses differently.
The aim is to protect the tax position of employees, which previously changed whenever expenses were reimbursed in full.
The aim is to encourage transfers to the northern offices, where staff shortages previously affected the company.
questions.explanation: The next sentence says employees will receive a lump sum 'rather than reimbursement of individual receipts', so the aim must be to end disputes over what is eligible. The others contradict the lump sum (receipts), concern tax, or are unrelated to expenses.
'Where a transferred employee leaves' introduces the specific case in which repayment applies; 'whereas' contrasts, 'wherein' means in which, and 'whereby' means by which.
To 'brief' a team about terms is to inform them in advance; 'debrief' refers to questioning after an event, and 'abridge' and 'abbreviate' mean to shorten.
